formal_name: Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus for Purposes of Educational Assessment and Instruction
description: The Delphi Report is the single most influential consensus document in the critical thinking field. Via a two-year Delphi process involving 46 experts across disciplines, Facione produced both a canonical definition and a detailed skill/disposition taxonomy that has shaped CT assessment instruments (including the CCTST and CCTDI) ever since.
canonical_definition: We understand critical thinking to be purposeful, self-regulatory judgment which results in interpretation, analysis, evaluation, and inference, as well as explanation of the evidential, conceptual, methodological, criteriological, or contextual considerations upon which that judgment is based.

ideal_critical_thinker_profile.description: The Delphi report generated the most detailed portrait of the 'ideal critical thinker' in the CT literature.
social_dimension: reasonable in the selection of criteria
persistent in seeking results as precise as the subject and the circumstances require

six_core_skills.definition: To comprehend and express the meaning or significance of a wide variety of experiences, situations, data, events, judgments, conventions, beliefs, rules, procedures, or criteria.

sub_skills.name: Categorization
sub_skills.description: Identifying the kind of claim, argument, or situation; assigning it to an appropriate category

sub_skills.name: Decoding Significance
sub_skills.description: Detecting the intended meaning behind statements, symbolic expressions, or behavioral data; understanding what something means in context

sub_skills.name: Clarifying Meaning
sub_skills.description: Removing ambiguity; specifying how a term is being used; unpacking the meaning of a complex statement

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 1 (Felt Difficulty) and Phase 2 (Intellectualization) — naming and framing the problem.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Information, Concepts, and Question-at-Issue elements

six_core_skills.definition: To identify the intended and actual inferential relationships among statements, questions, concepts, descriptions, or other forms of representation intended to express beliefs, judgments, experiences, reasons, information, or opinions.

sub_skills.name: Examining Ideas
sub_skills.description: Identifying the role ideas play in an argument; identifying similarities and differences among claims and questions

sub_skills.name: Detecting Arguments
sub_skills.description: Recognizing whether a passage contains an argument or merely assertions; identifying unstated conclusions

sub_skills.name: Analyzing Arguments
sub_skills.description: Identifying the stated and unstated premises; mapping the inferential structure; identifying the pattern of reasoning

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 3 (Hypothesis Formation) — structuring the elements of inquiry.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Information, Assumptions, and Inference elements

six_core_skills.definition: To assess the credibility of statements or other representations which are accounts or descriptions of a person's perception, experience, situation, judgment, belief, or opinion; and to assess the logical strength of the actual or intended inferential relationships among statements, questions, descriptions, or other forms of representation.

sub_skills.name: Assessing Claims
sub_skills.description: Judging whether a statement is credible; evaluating the reliability of sources and evidence

sub_skills.name: Assessing Arguments
sub_skills.description: Judging whether the logical form of the argument is valid; whether the premises are acceptable; whether the premises are relevant and sufficient to support the conclusion

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 5 (Testing) — evaluating whether the hypothesis holds up to scrutiny.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Intellectual Standards application across all elements

six_core_skills.definition: To identify and secure elements needed to draw reasonable conclusions; to form conjectures and hypotheses; to consider relevant information and to draw out the implications carried by data, statements, principles, evidence, judgments, beliefs, opinions, concepts, descriptions, questions, or other forms of representation.

sub_skills.name: Querying Evidence
sub_skills.description: Identifying the appropriate type of evidence needed; questioning the adequacy of available evidence; designing ways to gather relevant evidence

sub_skills.name: Conjecturing Alternatives
sub_skills.description: Forming multiple plausible hypotheses about what explains the evidence; generating rival hypotheses rather than accepting the first

sub_skills.name: Drawing Conclusions
sub_skills.description: Identifying the best-supported conclusion; recognizing when evidence is insufficient for a strong conclusion; drawing probabilistic rather than categorical conclusions when appropriate

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 4 (Reasoning) — drawing out the implications of hypotheses.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Interpretation/Inference and Implications/Consequences elements

six_core_skills.definition: To state and to justify that reasoning in terms of the evidential, conceptual, methodological, criteriological, and contextual considerations upon which one's results were based; and to present one's reasoning in the form of cogent arguments.

sub_skills.name: Stating Results
sub_skills.description: Accurately describing the conclusion reached; clearly articulating what one believes and why

sub_skills.name: Justifying Procedures
sub_skills.description: Explaining why particular methods, criteria, or conceptual frameworks were used in the inquiry

sub_skills.name: Presenting Arguments
sub_skills.description: Constructing well-formed arguments; anticipating objections; organizing reasoning for communication to others

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 5 (Testing) and the communicative dimension of reflection.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Purpose, Point of View, and all elements as they are communicated to others

six_core_skills.definition: Self-consciously to monitor one's cognitive activities, the elements used in those activities, and the results educed, particularly by applying skills in analysis, and evaluation to one's own inferential judgments with a view toward questioning, confirming, validating, or correcting either one's reasoning or one's results.

sub_skills.name: Self-Examination
sub_skills.description: Reflecting on one's own beliefs, values, and reasoning processes; identifying one's own biases; asking whether one's own reasoning meets the standards one applies to others

sub_skills.name: Self-Correction
sub_skills.description: Revising conclusions when new evidence warrants; correcting reasoning errors when identified; updating beliefs in light of good arguments

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Maps to Dewey's metacognitive dimension — the reflective awareness that supervises all phases of inquiry.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Intellectual Traits/Virtues, particularly Intellectual Humility and the ongoing application of standards
six_core_skills.special_note: Self-regulation is described as the 'master skill' — it is the skill that makes all other skills function as critical thinking rather than mere analytical competency.

cctdi_dispositions.name: California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory
cctdi_dispositions.description: The dispositional component of the Delphi consensus, developed into a psychometric instrument. Measures 7 traits independently, recognizing that someone can be skilled but not disposed, or disposed but not skilled.

seven_dispositions.description: Eagerness to seek the best knowledge even if that knowledge challenges one's preconceptions or comfortable beliefs
Tolerance of divergent views; sensitivity to the possibility of one's own bias
behavioral_markers: seeks out perspectives that challenge one's own

seven_dispositions.description: Prizing the application of reasoning and the use of evidence even for problems that present difficulty
behavioral_markers: uses evidence to approach complex problems

seven_dispositions.description: Valuing organization, focus, and diligence in inquiry
behavioral_markers: pursues inquiry with order and thoroughness

seven_dispositions.description: Trusting one's own reasoning processes and the conclusions reached through fair application of CT
behavioral_markers: leads others in inquiry when appropriate
makes decisions based on one's own reasoning
defends well-reasoned conclusions under social pressure

seven_dispositions.description: Intellectual curiosity — valuing acquiring knowledge and learning for its own sake
behavioral_markers: curious about wide range of topics

seven_dispositions.description: Prudent judgment; awareness that multiple perspectives are valid; understanding that sometimes conclusions must be reached despite uncertainty
behavioral_markers: accepts uncertainty as the condition of inquiry
applies appropriate epistemic standards to different domains
makes decisions despite incomplete information when required

skill_disposition_interaction.key_insight: Delphi explicitly distinguishes CT skills (cognitive) from CT dispositions (affective). A person may have the skills but not be disposed to use them, or be disposed but lack the skills. The ideal critical thinker exhibits both.

interaction_matrix.high_skills_high_dispositions: Master critical thinker — uses skills readily and accurately
interaction_matrix.high_skills_low_dispositions: Skilled but intellectually undisciplined — capable but unmotivated
interaction_matrix.low_skills_high_dispositions: Well-intentioned but ineffective — motivated but unable to execute
interaction_matrix.low_skills_low_dispositions: Uncritical thinker — neither capacity nor inclination

app_usage.exercise_feature: 6 core skills as exercise categories — each skill generates distinct exercise types
app_usage.progress_tracking: Skills map cleanly to learner progress metrics
app_usage.template_feature: Explanation sub-skills as template for written reflections (Stating Results, Justifying Procedures, Presenting Arguments)
